prompt: By the lesson, what turns a metric into a KPI?
hint: The word that matters is "key".

choices.text: Being shown on the main dashboard, in a larger font than the rest
choices.why: Where a number is drawn says nothing about whether anybody acts on it.

choices.text: It tracks an objective, and a named person acts on it when it moves
choices.why: Right: key to an objective and key to somebody's decisions; remove either and it is a metric again.

choices.text: A precise written definition
choices.why: Every metric needs one too. The definition makes it a metric, not a KPI.

choices.text: Being computed automatically rather than by hand
choices.why: How it is computed is plumbing; Varanda's systems produce hundreds of numbers automatically.

prompt: Online conversion is on Renata's weekly KPI page. What is it to Helena, by the lesson?
hint: "Key" is relative to a person.

choices.text: Also a KPI, because a KPI is a KPI for the whole company
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: the same number can be key on one page and a metric on another.

choices.text: A vanity number she ought to ignore
choices.why: Conversion drives sales; Helena uses it, just not as the number she acts on directly.

choices.text: A metric she opens when sales against plan disappoint
choices.why: Right: she does not act on it directly; it explains the KPI she does act on.

choices.text: Little, since a CEO looks at profit first
choices.why: Helena's KPI is sales against plan, and she does look below it.

prompt: Marketing wants "registered customers since 2015" on the KPI list, because it serves the objective of growing the online shop. By the lesson's three questions, what is still missing?
hint: The third question weeds out most candidates.

choices.text: A target, because a KPI without a target is a metric
choices.why: A target comes after the number has earned its place; this one has not yet.

choices.text: Someone who would do something different when it moves
choices.why: Right: the objective is there, but nobody would act on it; a total that only grows tells nobody what to change.

choices.text: A data source
choices.why: The number is easy to get from the e-commerce platform; data is not what it lacks.

choices.text: Nothing: serving an objective is what makes a number key
choices.why: That is only the first of the three questions; the other two ask who acts and what they would do.

prompt: Every KPI is a ___, and very few of them are KPIs.
hint: A quantity measured with a written definition.

prompt: In the week of 2 to 8 February, what share of delivered orders arrived within two days, in percent? (Renata's formula.)
hint: =ROUND(SUM(G2:G15)/COUNT(D2:D15)*100,1)

prompt: Why does the card count order 5111, cancelled on day 12 of a ten-day promise, in the denominator?
hint: What happened to that customer before they cancelled?

choices.text: Because every cancelled order belongs in the denominator
choices.why: The card excludes 5107, cancelled on day 1 before anything was late.

choices.text: Because furniture orders weigh more than parcels
choices.why: The card counts orders, not their size; 5111 is in for what happened to it, not for what it was.

choices.text: To make the rate come out lower and so look more cautious
choices.why: The card chooses a definition for what it means, not for the direction it moves the number.

choices.text: The customer waited past the date and gave up
choices.why: Right: leaving it out would reward the warehouse for a delay bad enough to lose the sale.

prompt: Match each line of the delivery card to what it says.
hint: Three lines are the definition, one is an obligation.

pairs.right: orders delivered by the promised day
delivered plus cancelled after the promise

prompt: Who should the card name as the owner of "delivered on promise"?
hint: Who can be asked on Monday why it fell?

choices.text: Lívia, because she computes it
choices.why: Computing it is the analyst's part; the owner explains it and decides what to do.

choices.text: Caio Barreto
choices.why: Right: one named person who explains the number and decides on carriers and routes.

choices.text: The operations department as a whole
choices.why: A department cannot be asked why the number fell; the owner is one person, never a department.

choices.text: Each carrier, for its own deliveries
choices.why: Carriers move the number, but Varanda's KPI needs somebody inside Varanda to answer for it.

prompt: Suppose order 5104, the parcel that took 3 days, had arrived on day 2. Using the card's definition, what would the week's rate be, in percent to one decimal?
hint: One more on promise in the numerator; the denominator does not change.

prompt: Which of these is a leading indicator for Varanda's online sales?
hint: It moves before the month closes, and it drives the result.

choices.text: Online sales for last quarter
choices.why: That is the result itself, known after the fact: lagging.

choices.text: Profit for the year
choices.why: Profit arrives even later than sales; it is the most lagging of the three.

choices.text: This week's share of site visits that end in an order
choices.why: Right: conversion is a branch of the tree, known by Monday, and it multiplies straight into sales.

choices.text: The number of registered customers since the site opened
choices.why: It moves early, but nothing links it to this month's sales; an early number about nothing.

prompt: With visits and the average ticket where they were in 2025, conversion rises from 1.25% to 1.5%. By what percentage do online sales rise?
hint: The parts of a product move the result in proportion.

prompt: Renata's campaign raises visits by 25% and conversion falls from 1.25% to 1%, ticket unchanged. What does the tree say?
hint: Multiply the branches.

choices.text: Sales rose about 25%, following the visits
choices.why: That reads one branch alone; the fall in conversion cancels the rise in visits exactly.

choices.text: Sales did not move: R$ 15.61 million either way
choices.why: Right: 1.25 times the visits at four fifths of the conversion is the same number of orders.

choices.text: Sales fell, because conversion is the branch that counts most
choices.why: No branch counts more than another in a product; here the two changes cancel out.

choices.text: Nothing can be said until the month closes
choices.why: That is the point of a tree: the branches are known early and the arithmetic is exact.

prompt: A KPI tree ends at the drivers somebody can change directly, which is also where its ___ are named.
hint: Conversion has two of them.

prompt: Sônia draws a tree: "training hours drive customer satisfaction, which drives store sales". How does it differ from the online sales tree?
hint: One of them is true by arithmetic.

choices.text: It has fewer branches than the online tree, so it is less reliable
choices.why: The number of branches is not the issue; what joins them is.

choices.text: It mixes HR with sales, which a tree cannot do
choices.why: A tree can cross departments; conversion already has an owner in operations.

choices.text: Its arrows are a guess to check; the other is arithmetic
choices.why: Right: visits × conversion × ticket is sales by definition; training to satisfaction to sales is a guess.

choices.text: Satisfaction cannot be measured at all, so the tree is useless
choices.why: Satisfaction can be measured; the lesson asks for the link to be checked, not for the tree to be thrown away.

prompt: Put the steps of setting Caio's target in the order the lesson builds it.
hint: A target set before the definition gets met by changing the definition.
items: Write the definition on the card
Read how far the weekly history wanders
Set the goal and the action threshold
trap: Picking the goal first feels decisive, and it is exactly what invites meeting it by redefining the number.

prompt: Over the twelve weeks, the card's rate ran from 74.1 to 84 with a median of 80.35. Why is a goal of 81 a poor one?
hint: Count the weeks at or above 81.

choices.text: It was met in five of the twelve weeks by luck
choices.why: Right: a goal reached by luck in a normal week measures luck.

choices.text: It is not a round number
choices.why: Roundness is the lesson's example of a bad reason, not a requirement.

choices.text: It sits well below the competitor's 92% on time
choices.why: The competitor's number has an unknown definition and cannot set this one.

choices.text: It is above the median, so it can never be reached
choices.why: Half the weeks are above the median by definition; 81 was reached five times.

prompt: Six months on, the KPI is at 88% and the deliveries take as long as before. The furniture promise went from seven days to ten. What happened?
hint: Every target creates a second way of reaching it.

choices.text: The carriers improved and the target worked as designed
choices.why: The deliveries take as long as before, so nothing the customer feels improved.

choices.text: The history was too short to set a sound target
choices.why: A longer history would not stop the promise being moved.

choices.text: It was met only by moving the promise
choices.why: Right: the number rose and the service did not; lesson 11 picks up what to pair with it.

choices.text: The denominator changed because fewer orders were cancelled
choices.why: Nothing in the story says cancellations changed; the promise did.

prompt: An action threshold set inside the normal range of the history is an ___ that rings every month.
hint: Something that rings.

prompt: Helena reads that a competitor delivers "92% on time" and asks why Varanda is at 76.9%. What should Lívia find out first?
hint: The same week of Varanda's gave 83.3, 71.4 and 50.

choices.text: Which carriers the competitor uses
choices.why: Useful later, but the gap may not be real until the two numbers are measured alike.

choices.text: Whether 92% is a better target than 85%
choices.why: Choosing a target from a number of unknown definition is the benchmark trap.

choices.text: How they define it: denominator and exclusions
choices.why: Right: if it leaves out every cancellation, the comparable Varanda figure is 83.3, not 76.9.

choices.text: Nothing: a higher number from a rival is all the evidence needed
choices.why: Two numbers under one name are not evidence until the definitions match.

prompt: Which of these belong on a KPI card, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Definition, plumbing, obligations.

choices.text: What is excluded from the count
choices.why: Right: part of the definition, and one of the lines people fill in differently.

choices.text: The threshold at which somebody must act
choices.why: Right: one of the obligations that make it somebody's job.

choices.text: The chart type it should be drawn with
choices.why: The card defines the number; how it is drawn depends on who reads it and where.

choices.text: The source system it is read from
choices.why: Right: the plumbing, so anybody can recompute it.

choices.text: The names of everybody who receives it
choices.why: The card names one owner; a mailing list is not part of the definition.

prompt: Sônia proposes reviewing staff turnover every day "to catch problems early". By the lesson, what is wrong with that?
hint: What decides how often a KPI is read?

choices.text: Turnover data is personal data and may not be read daily
choices.why: HR data is personal, but that limits who sees it, not how often.

choices.text: Frequency follows the decision, and those are monthly
choices.why: Right: a number read more often than anybody can act on it produces anxiety rather than action.

choices.text: A daily turnover figure would need a second owner
choices.why: The owner stays one person whatever the frequency.

choices.text: Turnover is a leading indicator and leading indicators are read monthly
choices.why: Turnover for the year is lagging, and the frequency rule is about decisions, not about the kind of indicator.

prompt: Renata wants her two-day figure, 50%, kept somewhere. What should Lívia do with it, by the lesson?
hint: It is not wrong; it is not Caio's KPI either.

choices.text: Delete it, so that the card's number stands on its own
choices.why: The lesson keeps it: a fair metric for parcels, on her own page.

choices.text: Let it replace the card's number, being the stricter of the two
choices.why: Strictness is not the test; it punishes furniture for a promise nobody made.

choices.text: Keep it on her page, labelled as a parcels metric
choices.why: Right: what the card prevents is two numbers under one name in the same meeting.

choices.text: Average it with Caio's 83.3 to settle the argument
choices.why: The average of two definitions is a third number with no definition at all.
